lessons.title: Why meat is inspected and who is involved
lessons.html:
The purpose of meat inspection

Meat inspection protects people who eat meat, protects the national herd and supports trade. In South Africa it is governed by the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and the regulations made under it, while animal disease control falls under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Every animal slaughtered at a registered abattoir must be inspected before and after slaughter, and only meat that passes may be marked and sold.

Main aims

  • Remove meat that is unsafe because of disease, parasites, contamination or residues.
  • Detect notifiable and controlled diseases such as tuberculosis, anthrax or foot-and-mouth disease and report them to state veterinary services.
  • Check that animals were handled humanely, as required by the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962.
  • Give feedback to farmers, for example about liver fluke, measles or bruising, so they can improve their herds.

The people in the system

The meat examiner or meat inspector works on the line and carries out routine inspection of heads, offal and carcasses. A veterinarian supervises, decides on difficult cases and makes final judgements on detained carcasses. The abattoir owner is responsible for hygiene, facilities and the hygiene management system. Provincial veterinary services audit the abattoir and enforce the law.

Your role as a meat examiner

You must work independently from production pressure. Line speed must never stop you from inspecting properly. If you cannot inspect a carcass because it is moving too fast or is dirty, you have the right and the duty to stop the line or detain the carcass. Your decisions are recorded, and they can be checked during an audit. Honest, consistent work is the basis of trust in the South African meat supply.

lessons.title: Ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection
lessons.html:
Two stages of inspection

Inspection happens in two stages. Both are required by law, and a carcass cannot be passed without them.

Ante-mortem inspection (before slaughter)

Animals are inspected in the lairage, normally on the day of arrival and again if they are held over. You look at every animal at rest and in motion. Check:

  • Movement and posture: lameness, stiffness, staggering, recumbency.
  • Breathing: coughing, laboured breathing, nasal discharge.
  • Body condition, swellings, wounds, abscesses, skin lesions.
  • Behaviour: excitement, depression, signs of nervous disease.
  • Cleanliness of the hide or fleece, and identification marks or ear tags.

Possible decisions are: pass for normal slaughter, slaughter under special conditions (for example at the end of the day), detain for further observation, or reject. Suspected notifiable disease must be reported to the veterinarian immediately and the animal kept apart.

Post-mortem inspection (after slaughter)

Post-mortem inspection uses three methods:

  1. Viewing the surfaces of the carcass and organs for colour, bruises, abscesses and contamination.
  2. Palpation (feeling) organs such as lungs and liver for hard nodules or abnormal texture.
  3. Incision of lymph nodes and selected muscles and organs, for example to look for cysts of measles.

The head, offal and carcass of one animal must stay identified together, using tags or synchronised rails, until the final judgement is made. If you find a lesion on the offal you must be able to find the matching carcass.

Hygiene during inspection

Sterilise your knife in the hot water steriliser after every carcass and after cutting into any abscess or diseased tissue. Wash hands and aprons regularly. A dirty inspection knife spreads contamination from one carcass to the next.

lessons.title: Judgement, marking and records
lessons.html:
Making a judgement

After inspection each carcass and its parts receive a judgement. The main outcomes are:

JudgementMeaning
PassedFit for human consumption and marked with the approved mark.
Partially condemnedAffected parts are cut away and condemned; the rest is passed.
DetainedMoved to the detention rail for further examination by the veterinarian or senior inspector.
Totally condemnedThe whole carcass and offal are unfit and must be destroyed.
Conditionally passedPassed only after a treatment such as freezing, where the regulations allow it.

Localised and generalised conditions

A key skill is to decide whether a condition is localised (one bruise, one abscess, one fluke-damaged liver) or generalised (spread through the body, with fever, enlarged lymph nodes throughout, or poor bleeding). Localised conditions usually lead to trimming or condemning the affected part. Generalised conditions usually lead to total condemnation.

Marking

Passed carcasses are marked with the approved stamp using food-grade ink. Stamps must be kept locked away when not in use so they cannot be misused. Condemned material is marked or stained so it cannot re-enter the food chain.

Records

Record every condemnation with the carcass number, owner, condition found and parts condemned. These records are used for farmer feedback, disease surveillance and audits. Report notifiable diseases to the state veterinarian without delay.

Key points

  • Meat inspection is required by the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and protects consumers and the national herd.
  • Every animal gets ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection.
  • Post-mortem inspection uses viewing, palpation and incision.
  • Keep head, offal and carcass identified together until judgement.
  • Localised conditions are trimmed; generalised conditions usually mean total condemnation.
  • Sterilise your knife between carcasses and record every finding.

quiz.question: What are the three methods of post-mortem inspection?
A carcass shows enlarged lymph nodes throughout the body and signs of fever. What is the most likely judgement?

options.text: Pass after trimming one lymph node
Total condemnation, as the condition is generalised

quiz.question: Why must head, offal and carcass stay identified together?

options.text: So that the hide can be sold
So that a lesion found on offal can be linked to the right carcass
So that the carcass weighs more
